15.text: better. I must say also, that, for the reindeer-breeder, the wolf and the evil spirit are a pair. One

16.text: spring I could not keep my herd together. It was at the end of spring. About that time the earth

17.text: begins to free itself from snow, and the reindeer like to scatter in all directions. The reindeer-

18.text: breeders call this time ‘greedy fuss’ (čipčiˊñɪlet). This time is terrible for all. On account of my

19.text: inability (to manage the reindeer), I spoke thus foolishly. When I was younger, I could assuage

20.text: my anger by outrunning the reindeer. That time I spoke foolishly because I felt my weakness:

21.text: ‘Here wolves, catch them and eat them!’ After a while I gave a ransom for these words, —

22.text: slaughtered some reindeer, and I also slaughtered one of my driving-reindeer that was very dear

23.text: to me. It was the first time that I spoke such foolish words.”¹

29.text: In the year 1898, in the Eskimo village Uñiˊsak, an old man was shot

30.text: at his own request. He was shot from behind. This is the only case of

31.text: voluntary death known to me, where the death-stroke was dealt from behind.

32.text: W. H. Dall, quoting a man named Noakum, a native of Plover Bay,

33.text: describes the killing of old men in the following manner: “Old and useless

34.text: people frequently ask to be put to death. The victim is taken to the place

35.text: of the dead, and an oval of stones is built. A large head-stone is placed at

36.text: one end, and another large stone at the foot; under these, two poles are laid

37.text: with thongs attached. A deer is killed, and the blood allowed to flow on the

38.text: head-stone. The victim is then placed on his back. The legs and arms of

39.text: course extend over the stone oval, and are tied to the poles, so that motion

40.text: is impossible. He is then asked if he is ready for death. If the answer is

41.text: affirmative, his nostrils are stopped up with a substance which stupefies him.

42.text: If the answer is negative, the deer-meat, which is otherwise eaten, is burned

43.text: as a kind of atoning-service.” Dall describes part of these doings as an eye-
